clinicalPearls: Tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome) is marked abnormal dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi due to atrophy or deficiency of the elastic and smooth muscle of the airway wall.
The dilated airway is abnormally compliant, so it collapses on expiration and cough, impairing clearance and predisposing to recurrent infection and bronchiectasis.
Corrugation of the airway wall between the cartilage rings produces mucosal outpouchings (tracheal diverticulosis), classically giving a scalloped contour on imaging.
It usually presents in adult men with chronic productive cough, recurrent lower respiratory infection, breathlessness and, in some, a loud ineffective cough.
Diagnosis rests on measuring the tracheal and main bronchial diameters on CT, which exceed defined upper limits of normal.
Dynamic imaging or bronchoscopy demonstrates the excessive expiratory collapse that accompanies the fixed dilatation.
Associations include connective-tissue and cartilage disorders (such as Ehlers-Danlos and cutis laxa) and, in children, certain congenital syndromes.

Management is largely supportive — airway clearance, prompt treatment of infection and immunisation — as no therapy reverses the structural abnormality; positive-pressure support may aid selected patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Tracheobronchomegaly results from deficiency or atrophy of the elastic fibres and smooth muscle within the membranous and cartilaginous portions of the tracheal and main bronchial walls. The weakened wall dilates progressively under normal transmural pressures, and the redundant, poorly supported tissue between cartilage rings herniates outward to form the characteristic corrugations and diverticula. The enlarged, flaccid airway loses its structural rigidity and collapses during expiration and coughing; because cough depends on generating high linear airflow velocities in a stable airway, the dynamic collapse renders cough ineffective and severely impairs mucus clearance. Retained secretions and recurrent infection damage the distal airways, producing bronchiectasis and further inflammation in a self-perpetuating cycle. The condition may be idiopathic, familial, or associated with heritable connective-tissue disorders in which generalised deficiency of elastic tissue affects the airway as one of several sites.
additionalDifferentials: bronchiectasis from other causes (cystic fibrosis, post-infective, immunodeficiency)
tracheomalacia or excessive dynamic airway collapse without dilatation
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with recurrent infection
acquired tracheal dilatation adjacent to fibrotic lung disease (traction)
additionalInvestigations: chest CT with measurement of tracheal and main bronchial diameters
dynamic expiratory CT to demonstrate excessive airway collapse
flexible bronchoscopy to assess wall flaccidity, diverticula and collapse
pulmonary function testing including flow-volume loop analysis
sputum culture and assessment of bronchiectasis-related infection
evaluation for associated connective-tissue or cartilage disorder
assessment of immune function where recurrent infection is prominent
redFlags: recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections with clinical deterioration
progressive respiratory failure from ineffective cough and secretion retention
acute large-airway obstruction from retained secretions or mucus plugging
features of a systemic connective-tissue disorder requiring broader assessment
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: some patients remain stable with mild symptoms for years, whereas those with extensive bronchiectasis and recurrent infection may progress to chronic respiratory impairment; management is supportive, as the structural airway abnormality is not reversible.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis by not measuring airway calibre on CT in a patient with recurrent infection and bronchiectasis.
Attributing the ineffective cough and recurrent infection solely to bronchiectasis without recognising the underlying megatrachea.
Relying on static imaging and missing the dynamic expiratory collapse.
Inserting airway stents without strong indication, given the poor structural support and complication risk.
Failing to screen for an associated heritable connective-tissue disorder.
